title: The New Teacher Experience
author: Angela Langlands
summary: Angela Langlands tells the story of Bettina, a composite new teacher who joined an established learning community team and struggled because she was handed the finished system without the history that produced it. Faced with an unfamiliar model, Bettina clung to what she knew, which Langlands says is a normal reaction, while the team also doubled down on its own comfort. The key diagnosis is that the team gave students a beginning-of-year boot camp but never gave adults the equivalent. Her fix is a hands-on onboarding in which a newcomer spends a couple of weeks moving between rooms, co-teaching, adding anecdotal notes and joining end-of-day debriefs about why each choice was made. She advises new teachers to ask for such a boot camp, tells administrators it needs flexible home bases rather than a new budget line, and suggests solo, pair and team actions. Once newcomers understand the how and the why, she argues, they help improve the model.
points: New teachers on an established team often cling to old habits because the system arrives without the understanding that built it, so resistance is a predictable response rather than a character flaw.
Schools that onboard students carefully often forget to do the same for adults, who need explanation of the why, not just routines.
An effective boot camp is hands-on co-teaching across rooms, shared record-keeping and a daily debrief on the reasons behind each decision.
Administrators can arrange it by sharing students across homerooms for a few weeks, so it costs flexibility rather than money.
Newcomers who understand the model start shaping it, as Bettina did when she suggested teachers move rooms, not only students.
quotes: When people don’t know what to do, they double down on what feels comfortable, because it gives them some control.
She was expected to join a well-oiled machine without the backbone of the understanding that built it.
We didn’t put Bettina through a teacher version of “boot camp.” We gave her the finished system, some brief information, and then said, “Let’s go!
What she needed was what a student teacher gets in a practicum. Theory only takes you so far, and it isn’t until a teacher is in the room with a master teacher that the theory starts to make sense.
At the end of the school day (or sometimes over lunch) comes the debrief about why we made each choice. The “why” conversation matters as much as the observing.
Once a newcomer has been through boot camp and understands the model, their insights, perspectives, and ideas shape the next version of what the community becomes.
Your feelings are justified. If you’ve joined a team that already works like a community and you feel lost, that doesn’t mean you’re failing.
We built the plane while flying it. That taught us everything. But the next teacher to board shouldn’t have to learn to fly mid-air.
